title: Implement and manage physical security
summary: Physical security protects people, facilities, equipment, media, and operations through layered deterrence, prevention, detection, response, and recovery controls that are maintained in their real environment.
outcome: Given a facility and threat scenario, select layered physical controls, define operational ownership and response, and verify that access, environmental, power, fire, and monitoring measures work together.
managerMindset: Physical controls are operational systems with owners, maintenance, detection, response, and evidence—not static construction features.

sections.title: Protect perimeter and internal areas in layers
sections.body: Physical security can combine site selection, perimeter barriers, lighting, locks, guards, badges, visitor control, mantraps, cameras, intrusion detection, restricted zones, equipment protection, and environmental safeguards. Perimeter security controls manage approach, boundaries, vehicles, people, and initial detection; internal security controls divide and monitor zones, rooms, racks, media, and movement. Layering should reflect threat, asset value, safety, privacy, and operational need; a control that creates unsafe egress or an unmonitored exception can introduce new risk. Define who monitors, responds, maintains, and reviews each layer.
keyPoints: Deterrent, preventive, detective, and response functions should be explicit at both perimeter and internal boundaries.
Critical areas need stronger boundaries and independent monitoring than general work areas.
Safety and emergency egress must not be sacrificed for security convenience.

sections.title: Operate environmental and physical-access controls
sections.body: Physical operations include badge lifecycle, visitor and escort procedures, key management, CCTV and alarm health, guard escalation, fire detection and suppression, HVAC, water, power, generator or UPS support, and maintenance access. Test access and environmental controls, protect their logs and management interfaces, and account for single points of failure. Coordinate facilities, security, IT, safety, emergency services, and business owners in the response plan. A failed sensor or reader is a control exception requiring an owner, compensating measure, expiry, and validation.
keyPoints: Physical access events can support logical investigations and must be attributable.
Environmental controls protect availability and safety as well as confidentiality.
Maintenance and emergency access need authorization, supervision, and closure evidence.

workedExamples.title: Data-center loading dock
workedExamples.situation: A contractor can reach a loading dock adjacent to a server room, and the camera covering the corridor has been offline for two weeks.
workedExamples.reasoning: Treat the camera outage as a control exception, restore or compensate for detection, review badge and visitor logs, verify zone boundaries and escort procedures, and assess whether the contractor's access should be restricted until coverage is restored. Document the owner, risk, duration, and validation.

distinctions.difference: Access control governs entry or movement decisions; physical security operations maintain layers, monitor events, respond, and protect environmental and facility functions.
Deterrence influences behavior by increasing perceived difficulty or consequence; detection identifies activity so the organization can respond.

misconceptions.misconception: A locked door is sufficient for a critical facility.
misconceptions.correction: Critical facilities need layered access, monitoring, environmental, power, fire, maintenance, and response controls.

misconceptions.misconception: Physical security logs are unrelated to cyber investigations.
misconceptions.correction: Entry, visitor, device, camera, and environmental evidence can establish presence, timing, and attack paths.

recallChecks.prompt: What functions should a physical security layer provide?
recallChecks.answer: Appropriate combinations of deterrence, prevention, detection, response, and recovery.

recallChecks.prompt: Why monitor control health as well as security events?
recallChecks.answer: A failed camera, reader, alarm, power, or environmental control creates a blind spot or availability risk.
Authorization, scope, identity, supervision or monitoring, time bounds, and closure evidence.

scenarioSeeds.scenario: A fire-suppression maintenance window temporarily disables an alarm zone.
scenarioSeeds.decision: Use an approved impairment process with fire safety authority, compensating detection or guard coverage, communication, expiry, and post-maintenance test.
scenarioSeeds.why: Temporary safety-control impairment needs the same rigor as a technical security exception.

studyPlan.learn: Study physical layers, perimeter and entry controls, zones, cameras, alarms, environmental safeguards, power, fire, and maintenance.
studyPlan.connect: Connect D7.14 to D3 facility design, D5 physical access, D2 media, and D7.2 monitoring.
studyPlan.apply: Inspect a facility diagram and identify control, response, maintenance, and evidence owners.
studyPlan.revisit: Explain how a physical control outage could become a cyber or availability incident.

review.notes: Independent AI review only. Claim evidence, exact content fingerprints, scope checks, visual and memory-map assessments are recorded in knowledge/quality/. No human expert review or exam-readiness claim.

visualLearningContract.teachingQuestion: At which physical boundary should a control prevent, detect, or record access/environmental harm, and who must respond?
visualLearningContract.misconception: A camera, badge reader, or sensor protects an asset by itself.
visualLearningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.
visualLearningContract.focalInsight: Boundary, authorization, zone separation, monitoring, environmental protection, and compensating control for a failed device.
visualLearningContract.intentionalOmissions: Do not prescribe a universal device model, retention duration, guard staffing level, or building code requirement.
visualLearningContract.retrievalPrompt: A visitor tailgates into a server corridor while a door sensor is offline. Identify the boundary, missed control, compensating measure, and evidence needed.
visualLearningContract.textFallback:
physical security: The coordinated protection of people, facilities, equipment, media, and environmental conditions through physical layers and operations.. Decision: Select layered controls from asset value, threat, safety, privacy, and operational need; assign monitoring and response ownership.. Failure/example: Installing devices with no monitoring or maintenance produces an appearance of protection, not a working control.
perimeter control: Control at or approaching the property/building boundary that channels, deters, detects, or restricts entry and movement.. Decision: Use where the organization needs early detection or managed approach before access to the facility interior.. Failure/example: A perimeter with unmonitored gaps moves confrontation and detection closer to protected assets.
perimeter security controls: The set of outer-boundary measures such as barriers, lighting, gates, exterior entry controls, cameras, and intrusion sensors.. Decision: Layer controls so approach detection, delay, identification, and response suit the site threat and safety conditions.. Failure/example: Relying only on a fence without detection or response leaves a breach unnoticed.
entry control: The authorization and controlled flow of people or materials through a defined entrance, using methods such as badges, guards, locks, or visitor procedures.. Decision: Match identity assurance and escort requirements to the area’s risk while preserving safe emergency egress.. Failure/example: A locked door with informal tailgating defeats the authorization decision it is meant to enforce.
internal security controls: Controls inside the facility that restrict and monitor movement among rooms, zones, racks, media areas, and sensitive operations.. Decision: Use internal layers to enforce need-to-access after someone legitimately enters the building.. Failure/example: Treating lobby access as permission for a server room enables lateral physical movement.
security zone: A physically bounded area with a defined asset sensitivity, authorized population, entry conditions, and monitoring/response rules.. Decision: Create zones where access requirements change; document transitions and exceptions.. Failure/example: An undefined “secure area” leaves staff unable to enforce who may enter or escort visitors.
cctv: Closed-circuit video surveillance used to observe, deter, investigate, or verify activity in a defined field of view.. Decision: Place and secure cameras for needed coverage, privacy limits, recording availability, and response use; protect IP-connected cameras as systems.. Failure/example: A camera pointed away from the entry or with unavailable recording cannot corroborate a tailgating event.
intrusion detection: Sensors and alarms that identify unauthorized boundary or zone entry attempts, such as door, motion, beam, vibration, or gate sensors.. Decision: Choose sensing appropriate to the environment and connect it to monitored triage and escalation.. Failure/example: A motion sensor with no alarm response only records a problem after the intruder has acted.
environmental control: Physical safeguards that maintain conditions or limit hazards affecting people and equipment, including fire, HVAC, water, and power protections.. Decision: Select controls from environmental hazards and life-safety requirements, with facilities and emergency coordination.. Failure/example: An equipment room can remain access-controlled yet fail from heat, smoke, or water.
